claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Single-phase CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
Single-phase CoCrFeNiTi has favorable plasticity and machinability.
The low hardness and strength of single-phase CoCrFeNiTi arise from low lattice friction.
Low lattice friction in homogeneous CoCrFeNiTi permits easy dislocation glide.
Easy dislocation glide produces limited work or strain hardening.
A lack of nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries promotes high plasticity.
Phase decomposition in other high-entropy alloys is associated with changes in hardness.
A moderate annealing treatment can induce nanoscale compositional fluctuations, phase separation, or precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
The scale of thermally induced decomposition can depend on alloy composition and annealing temperature.
Annealing-induced precipitates or phase-separated regions would obstruct dislocation motion in CoCrFeNiTi.
Annealing-induced nanoscale features would increase the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi.
Annealing-induced nanoscale features would increase the compressive strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature and below temperatures at which dynamic recovery or recrystallization dominate.
The comparison should hold only when annealing avoids complete phase transformation and significant grain coarsening.
As-cast and annealed CoCrFeNiTi samples can provide a controlled comparison if phase constitution, nanoscale obstacles, hardness, and strength are measured.

contradictions.description: The boundary restricts loading to approximately the yield stress, whereas compressive strength, plasticity, and strain-hardening behavior generally require deformation at or beyond yield. The stated boundary therefore does not fully cover the proposed outcome measurements.
